en.title: Gemini 4 Carbon: A Developer's Guide
en.summary: Google has officially opened up Gemini 4 Carbon, built for deep reasoning and long-horizon Agent tasks, with a unified million-token context window and three adjustable reasoning depth levels. The article covers pricing, migration tips, and five practical pointers for putting it to work — worth a try.

en.title: Google releases its first decision model, Gemini Decision 1, taking first place in 7 of 9 tests with accuracy up to 92.2%
en.summary:
Unlike some new models that only present benchmark scores, Google also disclosed use cases for the Gemini Decisions API in its internal products.

Length: 3,571 characters; reading time: about 12 minutes.

Gemini Decision 1 is Google's first-generation model built specifically for decisions. It does not generate text; instead, it multimodally scores a closed set of options in a single forward pass. Its companion API supports three types of decision tasks—yes/no, multiple-choice, and standard scoring—covering text, image, audio/video, and PDF inputs.

Supports three types of structured decisions; with multimodal input, the cost is just $0.10 per million Tokens; outputs carry no Token charges.

Intended for AI architects, enterprise decision-system developers, and engineers building cost-sensitive LLM applications.

While the AI industry is still competing over who can generate more Tokens and who has stronger reasoning, Google has launched a new model that does not rely on generating answers one Token at a time.

Google has just officially released Gemini Decision 1, along with the Gemini Decisions API powered by the model. Unlike traditional generative large models, this model is purpose-built for fast decisions and does not require generating one Token at a time.
en.reason: Google's Gemini Decision 1 scores 92.2% on JevBench and ranks first in 7 of 9 tests by scoring closed option sets in one forward pass, with API pricing at $0.10 per million input tokens and no output charge.

en.title: From "Finding Knowledge" to "Understanding Constraints": Business Semantics, Preference Graphs, and Context Engineering in Travel Agent Practice | AICon Beijing
en.summary:
The hard part of an enterprise travel Agent is not just document retrieval; it must simultaneously understand employee preferences, corporate travel standards, approval conditions, and real-time bookable resources.

Word count: 1,709
Reading time: about 6 minutes

AI Agents are shifting from assistive tools to engineered roles that take on end-to-end enterprise tasks. The core challenges lie in defining task boundaries, accepting outcomes, and production-grade risk control. The engineering focus has moved from model invocation to context management, tool integration, execution environments, and feedback-loop design. Coding Agents have evolved into collaborators that can understand codebases, run tests, and work together on complex development tasks.

Putting Agents into production requires a clear list of tasks that can be handed over and acceptance criteria; engineering architecture determines real-world value more than model capability; permissions, cost, and risk control are prerequisites for scaling.

Intended for AI platform engineers, MLOps engineers, and enterprise architects

When Agents truly enter enterprise workflows, which work can be handed to AI? 50+ real-world case studies reveal the answer!

AI is moving from an assistive tool that answers questions toward a worker that understands goals, calls systems, and completes tasks. When Agents truly enter enterprise workflows, the question is no longer how to build AI, but which work can be handed to AI, how results are accepted, and how permissions, costs, and risks...
en.reason: Ctrip corporate travel CIO Wang Zheng uses the AgentONE architecture to show how a travel Agent recalls preferences by city via a knowledge graph, merges context through shared State, and validates transport-connection rules with targeted retries, moving from document retrieval to constraint-bound recommendations.

11 月 11 日早上，Cursor 发布 Projects 的多人版。Projects 里的活，由一个协调智能体拆开、派给一群写代码的智能体，这套分工 9 月 10 日第一版就有了。这次真正多出来的是另一件事：几个人的智能体现在能进同一个项目，共用一块任务看板、一套资料，遇到事还能互相通气。
Projects 在 Cursor 里干的事，是把一整件事交给一队智能体。里面有个协调智能体，干的是包工头的活，它自己不写代码，负责把活拆成几件，并行派给写代码的工人，做完再收回来给你检查。这一队人都在同一个工地上干活，工地本身跑在云端的一台机器上，合上笔记本也不停；有的活必须在本机跑，它就临时开一个本地智能体去办。这和上一篇聊的 DeepSeek Super-agent 原型是同一类分工，一个常驻的包工头（代码里叫 Router）带一群工人，包工头自己不动手。

en.title: Cursor Projects' multiplayer mode comes with plenty of caveats: your plan must include Cloud Agents, sharing requires a team account and version 3.26.13 or later, and it only works within the same team.
en.summary:
Cursor Projects multiplayer: what's added isn't more workers, it's more worksites

View the latest updates and join the conversation

On the morning of November 11, Cursor released the multiplayer version of Projects. The work inside Projects is broken down by a coordinator agent and dispatched to a group of coding agents — that division of labor first shipped on September 10. What's genuinely new this time is something else: several people's agents can now enter the same project, share one task board and one set of materials, and compare notes with each other when something comes up.

What Projects does in Cursor is hand an entire job to a team of agents. One of them is a coordinator agent doing the foreman's work: it doesn't write code itself, it splits the job into pieces, dispatches them in parallel to the coding workers, then collects the results for you to review. The whole crew works the same site, and the site itself runs on a machine in the cloud, so closing your laptop doesn't stop it; some jobs have to run on the local machine, so it spins up a local agent on the spot to handle them. This is the same division of labor as the DeepSeek Super-agent prototype discussed in the previous piece — a resident foreman (called Router in the code) leading a crew of workers, with the foreman never lifting a finger.

AI 进了生产，问题才刚开始
这两年，把 AI 放进生产，几乎成了每家公司的必修课。接入之后的事才难：流程要重来，账要重算，最后都落到一句：用了到底有没有效。
我的体会来自一个小得多的场面。我手头有个项目，代码几乎全部交给 AI，起初反复返工。后来改成管两头：入口处用任务卡写清做什么、不许碰什么、做到什么样算完；产出处逐条验收，合格才合并。返工随即降了下来。
其中多数技术细节我并不懂，项目却没有失控，管住它的是分工、标准、决策与责任。凡是让 AI 承担自己并不完全掌握的工作的人，都处在同样的位置：
不做执行，但要对结果负责。

en.title: Putting AI into Enterprise Production: What Counts as Effective?
en.summary:
How to Effectively Integrate AI Execution with Management Thinking

See the latest updates and join the conversation

Once AI Enters Production, the Problems Are Just Beginning

Over the past two years, putting AI into production has become almost a required course for every company. The hard part comes after adoption: processes have to be rebuilt, the numbers recalculated, and it all comes down to one question—does using it actually work?

My takeaway comes from a much smaller setting. I had a project where nearly all the code was handed to AI, and at first it meant constant rework. Then I switched to managing both ends: at the input, a task card spelling out what to do, what not to touch, and what counts as done; at the output, item-by-item acceptance, with merges only after passing. Rework dropped right away.

I don't understand most of the technical details, yet the project never spun out of control. What kept it in check was division of labor, standards, decisions, and accountability. Anyone who lets AI take on work they don't fully understand is in the same position:

Not doing the execution, but accountable for the result.

Scaling up to a company

The approach I used is management. When something is too big for one person to finish, you set goals, divide the work, allocate resources, verify results, and take responsibility for them. A shop floor supervisor isn't necessarily better at turning screws than the workers; management deals with the problems that inevitably arise once work is split up.

There are four such problems, and when the executor becomes AI, each one changes shape.

Direction drifts. People align through goals and standards; AI takes things literally and optimizes toward the acceptance criteria, so standards have to be nailed down and acceptance

en.title: Google releases its first decision model, Gemini Decision 1, taking first place in 7 of 9 tests with accuracy up to 92.2%
en.summary:
Unlike some new models that only present benchmark scores, Google also disclosed use cases for the Gemini Decisions API in its internal products.

Length: 3,571 characters; reading time: about 12 minutes.

Gemini Decision 1 is Google's first-generation model built specifically for decisions. It does not generate text; instead, it multimodally scores a closed set of options in a single forward pass. Its companion API supports three types of decision tasks—yes/no, multiple-choice, and standard scoring—covering text, image, audio/video, and PDF inputs.

Supports three types of structured decisions; with multimodal input, the cost is just $0.10 per million Tokens; outputs carry no Token charges.

Intended for AI architects, enterprise decision-system developers, and engineers building cost-sensitive LLM applications.

While the AI industry is still competing over who can generate more Tokens and who has stronger reasoning, Google has launched a new model that does not rely on generating answers one Token at a time.

Google has just officially released Gemini Decision 1, along with the Gemini Decisions API powered by the model. Unlike traditional generative large models, this model is purpose-built for fast decisions and does not require generating one Token at a time.
en.reason: Google's Gemini Decision 1 scores 92.2% on JevBench and ranks first in 7 of 9 tests by scoring closed option sets in one forward pass, with API pricing at $0.10 per million input tokens and no output charge.

en.title: From "Finding Knowledge" to "Understanding Constraints": Business Semantics, Preference Graphs, and Context Engineering in Travel Agent Practice | AICon Beijing
en.summary:
The hard part of an enterprise travel Agent is not just document retrieval; it must simultaneously understand employee preferences, corporate travel standards, approval conditions, and real-time bookable resources.

Word count: 1,709
Reading time: about 6 minutes

AI Agents are shifting from assistive tools to engineered roles that take on end-to-end enterprise tasks. The core challenges lie in defining task boundaries, accepting outcomes, and production-grade risk control. The engineering focus has moved from model invocation to context management, tool integration, execution environments, and feedback-loop design. Coding Agents have evolved into collaborators that can understand codebases, run tests, and work together on complex development tasks.

Putting Agents into production requires a clear list of tasks that can be handed over and acceptance criteria; engineering architecture determines real-world value more than model capability; permissions, cost, and risk control are prerequisites for scaling.

Intended for AI platform engineers, MLOps engineers, and enterprise architects

When Agents truly enter enterprise workflows, which work can be handed to AI? 50+ real-world case studies reveal the answer!

AI is moving from an assistive tool that answers questions toward a worker that understands goals, calls systems, and completes tasks. When Agents truly enter enterprise workflows, the question is no longer how to build AI, but which work can be handed to AI, how results are accepted, and how permissions, costs, and risks...

11 月 11 日早上，Cursor 发布 Projects 的多人版。Projects 里的活，由一个协调智能体拆开、派给一群写代码的智能体，这套分工 9 月 10 日第一版就有了。这次真正多出来的是另一件事：几个人的智能体现在能进同一个项目，共用一块任务看板、一套资料，遇到事还能互相通气。
Projects 在 Cursor 里干的事，是把一整件事交给一队智能体。里面有个协调智能体，干的是包工头的活，它自己不写代码，负责把活拆成几件，并行派给写代码的工人，做完再收回来给你检查。这一队人都在同一个工地上干活，工地本身跑在云端的一台机器上，合上笔记本也不停；有的活必须在本机跑，它就临时开一个本地智能体去办。这和上一篇聊的 DeepSeek Super-agent 原型是同一类分工，一个常驻的包工头（代码里叫 Router）带一群工人，包工头自己不动手。

en.title: Cursor Projects' multiplayer mode comes with plenty of caveats: your plan must include Cloud Agents, sharing requires a team account and version 3.26.13 or later, and it only works within the same team.
en.summary:
Cursor Projects multiplayer: what's added isn't more workers, it's more worksites

View the latest updates and join the conversation

On the morning of November 11, Cursor released the multiplayer version of Projects. The work inside Projects is broken down by a coordinator agent and dispatched to a group of coding agents — that division of labor first shipped on September 10. What's genuinely new this time is something else: several people's agents can now enter the same project, share one task board and one set of materials, and compare notes with each other when something comes up.

What Projects does in Cursor is hand an entire job to a team of agents. One of them is a coordinator agent doing the foreman's work: it doesn't write code itself, it splits the job into pieces, dispatches them in parallel to the coding workers, then collects the results for you to review. The whole crew works the same site, and the site itself runs on a machine in the cloud, so closing your laptop doesn't stop it; some jobs have to run on the local machine, so it spins up a local agent on the spot to handle them. This is the same division of labor as the DeepSeek Super-agent prototype discussed in the previous piece — a resident foreman (called Router in the code) leading a crew of workers, with the foreman never lifting a finger.

AI 进了生产，问题才刚开始
这两年，把 AI 放进生产，几乎成了每家公司的必修课。接入之后的事才难：流程要重来，账要重算，最后都落到一句：用了到底有没有效。
我的体会来自一个小得多的场面。我手头有个项目，代码几乎全部交给 AI，起初反复返工。后来改成管两头：入口处用任务卡写清做什么、不许碰什么、做到什么样算完；产出处逐条验收，合格才合并。返工随即降了下来。
其中多数技术细节我并不懂，项目却没有失控，管住它的是分工、标准、决策与责任。凡是让 AI 承担自己并不完全掌握的工作的人，都处在同样的位置：
不做执行，但要对结果负责。
放大到一家公司
我用的这套办法，就是管理。一件事太大，一个人做不完，就定目标、分工作、配资源、验结果、对结果负责。车间主任不一定比工人更会拧螺丝，管理管的是拆分之后必然出现的问题。

en.title: Putting AI into Enterprise Production: What Counts as Effective?
en.summary:
How to Effectively Integrate AI Execution with Management Thinking

See the latest updates and join the conversation

Once AI Enters Production, the Problems Are Just Beginning

Over the past two years, putting AI into production has become almost a required course for every company. The hard part comes after adoption: processes have to be rebuilt, the numbers recalculated, and it all comes down to one question—does using it actually work?

My takeaway comes from a much smaller setting. I had a project where nearly all the code was handed to AI, and at first it meant constant rework. Then I switched to managing both ends: at the input, a task card spelling out what to do, what not to touch, and what counts as done; at the output, item-by-item acceptance, with merges only after passing. Rework dropped right away.

I don't understand most of the technical details, yet the project never spun out of control. What kept it in check was division of labor, standards, decisions, and accountability. Anyone who lets AI take on work they don't fully understand is in the same position:

Not doing the execution, but accountable for the result.

Scaling up to a company

The approach I used is management. When something is too big for one person to finish, you set goals, divide the work, allocate resources, verify results, and take responsibility for them. A shop floor supervisor isn't necessarily better at turning screws than the workers; management deals with the problems that inevitably arise once work is split up.

There are four such problems, and when the executor becomes AI, each one changes shape.

Direction drifts. People align through goals and standards; AI takes things literally and optimizes toward the acceptance criteria, so standards have to be nailed down and acceptance
en.reason: Handing nearly all project code to AI caused repeated rework until task cards defined what to do, what not to touch and acceptance criteria, with line-by-line checks before merging, after which rework fell, framing enterprise AI production as management reform.
